description: Amanita pantherina, the Panther Cap, is a toxic and psychoactive mushroom of Europe and Asia recognized by its brown cap dotted with white warts, a ring on the stem, and concentric hoop-like volval rings at the swollen base. It contains the isoxazole compounds ibotenic acid and muscimol — the same toxins as the fly agaric (A. muscaria) — typically at higher and more variable concentrations.
edibilityNotes: Toxic and psychoactive — not edible. Contains ibotenic acid and muscimol, producing "pantherina syndrome": confusion, agitation, ataxia, delirium, drowsiness, and sometimes seizures or coma. Toxin levels are higher and more erratic than in A. muscaria, making poisoning more severe; fatalities are rare but reported. The principal real-world danger is mistaking the panther cap for the edible Blusher (Amanita rubescens) or for Amanita excelsa/spissa. It can also be confused with the fly agaric (A. muscaria), which shares the same toxins.
distribution: Widespread across Europe and Asia; closely related forms are reported in North America and elsewhere.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Amanita rubescens
dangerousLookalikes.note: The Blusher; edible only when thoroughly cooked. Flesh bruises and stains pinkish-red where cut or damaged, and it lacks the sharp concentric basal volval rings of A. pantherina. Foragers seeking the Blusher risk taking the toxic panther cap instead.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Amanita excelsa
dangerousLookalikes.note: Grey-brown European species (and its variety spissa), considered edible by some. Distinguished by greyish warts, a grooved ring, and a stem base lacking the sharp hoop-like marginal volval rings of A. pantherina; flesh does not redden as in the Blusher.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Amanita muscaria
dangerousLookalikes.note: The Fly Agaric; toxic and psychoactive, sharing the same isoxazole toxins. Typically red to orange cap (can fade to yellowish or brown), distinguishing it, but brown forms can be confused with A. pantherina.
